overview.title: Building the small Dogs vs. Cats subset (Listing 8.6, part 1)
overview.section: 8.2 Training a convnet from scratch on a small dataset
overview.main_topic: Context of the 2013 competition, dataset size, the rationale for subsampling, the target directory structure, and the first half of the copying utility
overview.central_idea: From the 25,000 labelled images, the authors build a deliberately small, balanced dataset: 1,000/500/1,000 images per class for train/validation/test, stored in a train|validation|test × cat|dog directory tree. A make_subset helper written with pathlib, os and shutil creates the directories and copies the files.
overview.importance: It defines the data every model in chapter 8 is trained and evaluated on. The class-subdirectory layout is what the directory-based loading utility on p.271 expects.
learning_objectives: Recall the dataset facts: 25,000 images, 12,500 per class, 543 MB compressed
Explain why the authors deliberately train on less than 10% of the available data
Describe the dogs_vs_cats_small directory structure and the per-folder counts
Understand the first part of make_subset: paths with pathlib and creating directories with os.makedirs
prerequisites: Basic Python file handling, pathlib's / operator

summary:
**Historical context.** The 2013 Kaggle Dogs vs. Cats competition was, "unsurprisingly", won by entrants using ConvNets, and the best entries reached **up to 95% accuracy**. The authors promise to get fairly close to this in the next section, while training on **less than 10%** of the data the competitors had.

**Dataset facts and subsampling.** The full dataset has **25,000 images** (12,500 per class) and is 543 MB compressed. From it the authors build a new dataset with three subsets:

| subset | per class | total |
|---|---|---|
| train | 1,000 | 2,000 |
| validation | 500 | 1,000 |
| test | 1,000 | 2,000 |

Why subsample? Many image datasets in practice contain only a few thousand samples, and more data would make the problem easier, so "it's good practice to learn with a small dataset".

**Directory structure.** The data goes in `dogs_vs_cats_small/`, with `train/`, `validation/` and `test/` folders, each holding `cat/` and `dog/` subfolders. Callouts give the counts (1,000 / 1,000, 500 / 500, 1,000 / 1,000). One folder per class is the convention that lets Keras infer labels from folder names later (p.271).

**Listing 8.6 (first half).** The authors use `shutil` ("a Python library for running shell-like commands") together with `os` and `pathlib`. `original_dir` points to `train` (where the original data was uncompressed) and `new_base_dir` to `dogs_vs_cats_small`. The helper `make_subset(subset_name, start_index, end_index)` copies cat (respectively, dog) images with indices in `[start_index, end_index)` into `new_base_dir/{subset_name}/cat` (resp. `dog`). On this page it loops over the two categories, builds the target path with pathlib's `/` operator, and calls `os.makedirs(dir)`. The filename construction, copy loop and the three calls (`train` 0-1000, `validation` 1000-1500, `test` 1500-2500) are on p.269.

concepts.name: Class-per-folder dataset layout
concepts.definition: Organizing images as split/class/image.jpg so labels are implied by folder names.
concepts.intuition: The folder an image lives in is its label.
concepts.technical: Keras' directory-based dataset loader infers class labels from subfolder names (used in 8.2.4, p.271).
concepts.significance: It is the input format for the data pipeline of this chapter.
concepts.misconception: The file name 'cat.0.jpg' is not what assigns the label; the folder is.

concepts.name: Train / validation / test subsets
concepts.definition: Separate data for fitting, for model selection/tuning, and for the final unbiased evaluation.
concepts.intuition: Practice exams, a mock exam, the real exam.
concepts.technical: Here: 2,000 / 1,000 / 2,000 images, disjoint index ranges per class.
concepts.significance: Disjoint ranges guarantee that no image appears in two subsets.
concepts.misconception: The test set should not be used for tuning, or it stops being an unbiased estimate.

concepts.name: Deliberately learning on small data
concepts.definition: Training on a subsample to mimic the common real-world small-data regime.
concepts.intuition: Training with weights on makes you better when it counts.
concepts.technical: 8% of available training data; overfitting becomes the main issue (p.266).
concepts.significance: It makes the effect of augmentation and transfer learning visible.
concepts.misconception: The authors are not saying small data is better; more data would make the problem easier.

code.title: Copying images to training, validation, and test directories (first part)
code.original_code:
import os, shutil, pathlib
original_dir = pathlib.Path("train")
new_base_dir = pathlib.Path("dogs_vs_cats_small")
def make_subset(subset_name, start_index, end_index):
    for category in ("cat", "dog"):
        dir = new_base_dir / subset_name / category
        os.makedirs(dir)
code.what_it_does: Sets up source and destination paths and begins the make_subset helper, which creates the per-class directory for a given subset. The rest of the function body (building filenames and copying) and the three calls continue on p.269.

deeper.title: Where the subset sizes come from
deeper.body: Per class: 1,000 + 500 + 1,000 = 2,500 images, so indices 0-2499 of each class are used out of 12,500. Totals: 5,000 of 25,000 images (20%). Training uses 2,000 / 25,000 = 8%, which matches the 'less than 10%' claim.

deeper.title: Why practise on less data?
deeper.body: It is like a musician practising on a cheap instrument. If you learn to get good results under constraints, the techniques (regularization, augmentation, transfer) carry over, and results get better when conditions improve.

takeaways: The 2013 competition winners used ConvNets and reached up to 95%; the chapter gets close using less than 10% of the data.
Full dataset: 25,000 images (12,500 per class), 543 MB compressed.
Subset per class: 1,000 train / 500 validation / 1,000 test, stored under dogs_vs_cats_small/{split}/{cat,dog}.
Learning with a small dataset is good practice because real datasets often only have a few thousand samples.

questions.question: How many cat images does dogs_vs_cats_small/validation/cat contain?
questions.explanation: The validation set has 500 samples of each class. 1,000 is the per-class count for train and test, and 12,500 is the per-class total of the full dataset.

questions.question: What fraction of the original data is used for training, and why do the authors use so little?
questions.answer: 2,000 of 25,000 images (8%, 'less than 10%'). Many real image datasets only have a few thousand samples, so it's good practice to learn with a small dataset.
questions.explanation: Both facts are on the page.

questions.question: Why is the class-per-subfolder layout (train/cat, train/dog, …) convenient?
questions.answer: The label of every image is implied by its folder, so a loading utility can infer labels from directory names without a separate label file.
questions.explanation: This is an inference about the next steps (directory-based loading on p.271); the page itself only shows the structure.

questions.question: In Listing 8.6, what does `new_base_dir / subset_name / category` produce?
options: A string containing only the category name
questions.explanation: pathlib overloads / to join path components. It is not arithmetic, and the file list is built separately on p.269.

questions.question: What happens if you run Listing 8.6 twice, and how could you fix it?
questions.answer: os.makedirs raises FileExistsError because the directories already exist. Delete the folder first or pass exist_ok=True.
questions.explanation: This is standard os.makedirs behaviour (an explanation beyond the book).

questions.answer: Up to 95%; 25,000 images, 12,500 per class, 543 MB compressed.
